results.title: CoreWeave Can Raise Prices Twice in Three Months. Can It Afford to Keep Building?
results.author: Jabran Kundi
highlights:
CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ: CRWV) has raised per-hour GPU prices twice, first by 25% across all products in July 2026 and then by another 10% over the past two to three months. UBS analyst Karl Keirstead sees the pricing gains as evidence that demand in the AI infrastructure market remains strong. However, such rapid growth comes with a heavy funding requirement. CRWV ranks No. 4 among our 11 AI Stocks That Will Go to the Moon. You won't want to miss the three stocks that claimed the top spots.

...

Analyst Karl Keirstead says the industry is seeing higher hosted Nvidia GPU prices and improving revenue per gigawatt of capacity. This supports a key part of the bull thesis, but their impact will take time to show up in financial statements. The fact that prices have increased twice within a few months suggests customers are willing to pay higher rates.

...

This is where the recent pricing increases become important. Together, they raise hourly pricing by about 37.5%. Any portion of that increase that flows through to sales would lower enterprise-value-to-sales multiple, assuming enterprise value remains unchanged. However, the news does not specify how much of the business is covered by the new pricing.

results.title: CRWV Stock Hits 17-Month Low Before Reversing Losses Amid Reported Plans For Another GPU Price Hike
results.author: Prabhjote Gill
highlights:
Prabhjote Gill Tue, October 20, 2026 at 10:58 AM EDT 4 min read

- According to a report by The Information, CoreWeave reportedly disclosed an additional 10% increase in hourly GPU pricing. 
- This comes after a roughly 25% increase across CoreWeave's products in July. 
- The company faces scrutiny over its debt burden and bond yields, with Reuters reporting about $50 billion in debt, including $24 billion in committed loans. 

CoreWeave (CRWV) shares fell to their lowest level in 17 months in morning trade on Tuesday before reversing losses as the AI names came back under renewed selling pressure. 

John McPeake, an analyst at Rosenblatt Securities, told The Information that the company disclosed an additional 10% increase in hourly GPU pricing at a customer conference in San Francisco several weeks ago. The reported increase would follow a broader price hike the company implemented in July.

...

## CoreWeave Reportedly Plans To Raise GPU Pricing Again 

CoreWeave raised prices by about 25% across its products in July, CFO Nitin Agrawal disclosed during the company's August second-quarter (Q2) earnings call. 

Agrawal said the increase was "an approximately 25% increase across SKUs in response to the current demand environment." He also said the company was passing higher component costs, including more expensive GPUs, on to customers in addition to the broader price increase. 

The latest reported increase was discussed at the San Francisco customer conference. Truist analyst Arvind Ramnani first wrote about it following the event in the first week of October. UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said the additional 10% increase had occurred over the preceding two to three months.

results.title: CoreWeave - CoreWeave Continues to Contract New Compute Capacity at Higher Prices
highlights:
CoreWeave - CoreWeave Continues to Contract New Compute Capacity at Higher Prices 

# News Details 

## CoreWeave Continues to Contract New Compute Capacity at Higher Prices 

 September 17, 2026 

 LIVINGSTON, N.J.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- CoreWeave, Inc. (Nasdaq: CRWV) today announced that since June 30, 2026, CoreWeave has continued to contract new compute capacity at higher prices. In the third quarter of 2026, CoreWeave has signed short-dated customer contracts of approximately three to six months, with pricing of approximately $40 million per megawatt, calculated as annualized revenue divided by power required to service the related clusters. Furthermore, as previously announced on its second quarter earnings call on August 11, 2026, CoreWeave added more than $25 billion of net new customer commitments early in the third quarter of 2026, which are not reflected in the revenue backlog as of June 30, 2026, and increased its total contracted power to approximately 4.2 gigawatts as of August 11, 2026 from approximately 3.7 gigawatts as of June 30, 2026.

results.title: CoreWeave's not-so-secret weapons: Price hikes and an Nvidia trump card - PitchBook
results.author: Emerson Smith
highlights:
Over the past week, neoclouds came under immense pressure driven by CoreWeave’s bond selloff. But the panic over CoreWeave will most likely prove premature: Neoclouds are well positioned to increase prices through at least 2028, and Nvidia’s support can calm investors in CoreWeave and potentially other neoclouds.

Rising prices signal demand remains strong. They also mean that CoreWeave and other cloud operators can increase cash flows, especially as contracts renew. 

A GPU supply-and-demand imbalance began last year and persisted through 2026. On its Q1 earnings call, CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said that “demand is accelerating across the board. Average pricing for the A100s, H100s, H200s, and L40s all increased quarter over quarter, and we remain largely sold out for near-term capacity across our fleet.” CoreWeave also shared in a September release that its new compute contracts are priced higher than before.

Similarly, Nebius called out higher pricing in Q2 and in Q3 they revealed deals with large customers whose upfront payments covered 50% to 60% of related capex, a rich source of capital.

...

We believe that CoreWeave has the ability to calm investors by increasing prices, slowing deliveries and improving its leverage metrics. It would grow more slowly but would protect itself from future bond and stock selloffs and, in doing so, signal strength to customers.

results.title: CoreWeave (CRWV) Is Charging More for AI Compute, and Customers Keep Paying
results.author: Maham Fatima
highlights:
On September 17, CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) said it has kept signing customers at higher prices since June 30. Its third quarter contracts run just three to six months, yet they price out around $40 million of annualized revenue per megawatt of power. That is a striking number for an AI cloud that is still losing money. The real question is whether pricing like that can eventually outrun the cost of building it all.

...

Start with price. CoreWeave describes the deals signed since June 30 as coming at higher rates, and $40 million of yearly revenue for every megawatt shows how much customers will pay to secure capacity. That is what pricing power looks like. Short contracts also mean pricing gets reset often, so the company can capture more if demand stays tight. 

Volume backs it up. The revenue backlog was about $104 billion on June 30. That excludes over $25 billion in fresh commitments added early in the third quarter, all money customers have promised to spend. Contracted power tells the same story, rising to about 4.2 gigawatts by the August 11 earnings call from about 3.7 gigawatts on June 30. And the customer base is widening, with enterprises like Caterpillar and Bentley Systems joining AI labs, while second-quarter revenue of $2,575 million more than doubled from $1,212 million a year earlier.

...

CoreWeave's September 17 update says customers are paying more for its capacity, and that is hard to ignore. What it does not show is whether higher prices can catch up with the interest bill and the build-out still ahead. Bulls need each short renewal to hold its price while new capacity comes online. Bears are waiting for delivery to slip or pricing to soften, since either would hit a company already in the red.

results.title: CoreWeave Stock Just Got a Jaw-Dropping Upgrade From JPMorgan
results.author: Nauman Khan
highlights:
This time, JPMorgan upgraded CoreWeave to “Outperform” from “Neutral” and raised its price target to $125 from $120. The bank especially points to a more favorable pricing environment for AI compute.

The call comes as demand for AI infrastructure remains strong while available capacity stays relatively tight. For CoreWeave, that could create room to charge more for shorter-term contracts and improve the economics of its rapidly expanding business.

...

This is the key part of the upgrade. JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee said compute pricing has improved during 2026, creating a more supportive backdrop for CoreWeave. The company raised prices on roughly 25% of its products in July, while competitors such as Nebius have also moved prices higher.

Short-term contracts offered by rivals are now reportedly priced at nearly three times CoreWeave’s rates on longer-term agreements. That gap could give CoreWeave an opportunity to shift more capacity toward shorter contracts carrying higher prices.

The company also completed a $5.5 billion delayed-draw term loan in August, giving it additional financing flexibility as it expands its infrastructure.

...

Moreover, CoreWeave’s recent partnership with Harell Data also adds to that story. Harell plans to use CoreWeave Cloud for AI training, fine-tuning, and inference workloads using Nvidia A100 and Hopper GPUs, expanding the company’s exposure to specialized enterprise AI demand.

results.title: Hit · GPU price rises live in new short contracts; CoreWeave’s fleet average still lags in Q3 — resolves 2026-11-16 — SecondSource
highlights:
Hit · GPU price rises live in new short contracts; CoreWeave’s fleet average still lags in Q3 — resolves 2026-11-16 — SecondSource

# GPU price rises live in new short contracts; CoreWeave’s fleet average still lags in Q3 — resolves 2026-11-16

GPU price rises live in new short contracts; CoreWeave’s fleet average still lags in Q3 — resolves 2026-11-16

Scheduled check 2026-11-16 · settled 2026-11-12

Our earlier call, under recheck · Written on Oct 18, 2026

Background

The debate is how tight AI compute really is in autumn 2026: seller presentations show sharp rises on new short contracts, while public pay-as-you-go price indexes rose far less. If only new short contracts are rising, a GPU renter’s total revenue will not keep pace at once, and anyone estimating fleet revenue from seller presentations will overshoot. SecondSource reads the premium as concentrated in new marginal contracts with the fleet average lagging, while the opposing reading says the whole fleet is being repriced.

The call

SecondSource’s reading: GPU tightness in autumn 2026 shows up as a premium tied to contract length. Short contracts of 3 to 6 months and cancellable large orders run about $40 million to $60 million per MW (a megawatt of data-center power) per year, while five-year contracts run only about $10 million to $16 million.

CoreWeave, a cloud company that rents out GPUs, says it raised prices about 25% across its products in July. But average revenue per MW across its whole fleet will not catch up with that marginal price soon; a rough calculation from second-quarter figures puts it at about $7 million to $8 million.

Our bet: third-quarter 2026 revenue, annualized and divided by end-of-quarter active power, will still be below $10 million per MW per year.

Sources behind the call

CoreWeave, Inc.(SEC EDGAR,accession 0001769628-26-000429) “~25% price increase across SKUs in July 2026”

The receipt

Grace period of 14 days after CoreWeave’s Q3 2026 earnings press release (expected mid-November 2026). Take the quarterly revenue stated in the release times 4, divided by the end-of-quarter active power (GW) stated in the same release, to get annualized revenue per MW.

Read the full deep dive

Outcome

Hit (settled 2026-11-12)

On 2026-11-12 this call was settled: it held. The prediction: in the third quarter of 2026, CoreWeave's annualized quarterly revenue divided by end-of-quarter active power would still be below $10 million per MW per year, meaning price rises are concentrated in new short contracts while the fleet average lags. How it would be checked, agreed in advance: take the quarterly revenue in CoreWeave's third-quarter results release, multiply by 4, and divide by the end-of-quarter active power stated in the same release. Below $10 million per MW per year would count as a hit; at or above it, a miss. The release came out on 2026-11-10: third-quarter revenue of $3,661 million, more than 200 MW added, and active power of over 1.7 GW. $3,661 million times 4 divided by 1,700 MW is about $8.61 million per MW per year, below the $10 million line, so the call held. The release says "over" 1.7 GW, which would only push the ratio lower, and the basis matches the 1.5 GW reported for the second quarter, so the voiding condition was not triggered. Limit: this shows only that the fleet average stays below the line. It does not confirm that new short contracts price at $40 million to $60 million per MW; that figure still comes from seller presentations.

results.title: Is GPU compute tight? The answer is in contract length | SecondSource
highlights:
Correction, November 4, 2026. The version first published on October 18 put a term premium in its headline and conclusion as the shape of the tightness, reading the whole 2.5-to-4-times gap between short and long contracts as tightness, and said CoreWeave's listed prices "have not moved"; those lines were corrected in place on October 18 and October 23. The conclusion is unchanged: GPU compute is tight, but the gap can only be called high, and how much tighter than in past years cannot be said.

...

That read the 2.5 to 4 times between CoreWeave's three-to-six-month contracts, about US$40 million per MW per year in its investor presentation, and our own estimate of US$10 million to US$16 million for five-year contracts, worked out from total contract values, as the tightness itself. Longer contracts are normally cheaper, so a gap by itself is normal, and the two ends are not the same company, chip generation or capacity basis. The body also called this autumn's multiple "steeper" than the public market's term discount without noting that the two compare different terms. Section four now ... the public ... as ... yard ... deploying ... 4 ... % below pay ... as ... you ... go about ... - ... Source ... s ... the ... 5 to ... times ... that, ... because the ... it ... only ... That rested on the October 18 reading matching an August third-party blog post and 2025 price guides; the pricing page keeps no archive, and the blog post is not among this piece's sources. Section two now says whether the listed price moved around July can't be checked, and that the 25% most likely went into contract prices because a listed-price change would touch only about 2% of revenue, which is our reading of the 10-Q and the pricing page.

...

## Key takeaways

CoreWeave, a cloud company that specializes in renting out GPUs, the chips AI runs on, says rental prices rose about 25% starting in July. Yet a public index that the website getdeploying compiles from the list prices on dozens of providers' websites read only a 5% rise over a year in mid-September. Both numbers can be right. Almost all of CoreWeave's revenue comes from customers on contracts, while the index collects only the hourly, stop-any-time prices listed on websites (pay-as-you-go), so the two numbers measure different prices. Where compute is visibly tight, with more would-be renters than machines, is contract length: customers who sign for only three to six months pay 2.5 to 4 times the price of a five-to-six-year contract. That is above the gap of about 2 times between renting by the hour and signing for three years in the public market (SecondSource's conversion), but the two multiples cover different terms, so the gap can only be called high. No multiple calculated the same way exists for earlier years, so how much tighter than in past years cannot be said. Long contracts also require 20% to 30% up front. In October, after another provider raised list prices, the index's one-year rise reached 18%. CoreWeave's third-quarter results will show how fast new prices lift the average price across all of CoreWeave's contracts.

...

On the August 11 earnings call, CoreWeave CFO Nitin Agrawal described "our July pricing changes which included an approximately 25% increase across SKUs" (call transcript; also the investor presentation attached to CoreWeave's US$3 billion convertible notes issue on September 17). An SKU is a product model.

In the same period, the getdeploying public index read only a 3.3% rise over four weeks and 5% over a year for the week of September 14. SecondSource's September 18 daily brief drew a conclusion from the gap: the tightness is concentrated in newly signed short-term contracts, out of sight of public prices.

...

A GPU can be rented in two ways. One is pay-as-you-go: the listed price on a provider's website, billed by the hour and stoppable at any time. The other is a contract price locked in for months or years, mostly under committed contracts that are paid whether or not the capacity is used. Hotels work the same way, with a rack rate posted at the front desk and a rate negotiated in a corporate contract.

CoreWeave's second-quarter 10-Q says 98% of revenue comes from committed contracts and only about 2% from pay-as-you-go. CoreWeave's pricing page lists the H100, one of NVIDIA's GPU models, at US$6.16 per GPU per hour, the figure read on October 18. The site keeps no older versions, so whether this price moved around July can't be checked. In the public index, CoreWeave also appears at US$6.16.

So the 25% most likely went into the prices of new and renewed contracts: even if the listed price did move, the change would touch only about 2% of revenue. The CFO did not say which kind of price the 25% refers to; this reading rests on the 10-Q and the pricing page. The two numbers also cover different periods, so the two cannot be compared directly: the 25% is one company's single price change in July, and the 5% is a year's rise in dozens of providers' listed prices.

...

At the shortest end among contracts, CoreWeave's September investor presentation puts three-to-six-month contracts signed in the third quarter at about US$40 million per MW per year. Assuming NVIDIA's newer-generation GB200 chips, that is about US$7.6 to US$8.4 per GPU per hour, while CoreWeave lists the same chip at US$10.50, so short contracts are expensive relative to long ones, not relative to list prices (the conversion is in the appendix). At the longest end, SecondSource found five contracts of five to six years with value, term and capacity all public, and divided total value by years and then by capacity. For example, under a contract between IREN, which rents out GPUs, and NVIDIA, IREN rents GPU computing in IREN's own data centers to NVIDIA for internal research: US$3.4 billion, 5 years, about 60 MW, which works out to about US$11.3 million per MW per year. The five contracts together fall between about US$10 million and US$16 million.

US$40 million divided by US$10 million to US$16 million means a short contract costs about 2.5 to 4 times a long one. The two ends come from different companies, so the multiple shows only the order of magnitude (the basis is in the appendix). Longer commitments are normally cheaper. For the provider, a customer locked in for five years means years of revenue secured in advance, which is worth a discount. A customer who can leave at any time leaves the provider carrying the risk of idle machines, so the unit price is higher. So the gap itself is normal; calling the market tight depends on how much bigger the gap is than normal, and the next section uses the public market as the yardstick.

...

For the week of October 12, getdeploying's reading became 9% over four weeks and 18% over a year; SecondSource's recomputation from getdeploying's public weekly data matches. In the same period Nebius, another GPU rental company, raised listed prices from October 1 (Nebius pricing page). The H100 went from US$3.85 to US$4.50 an hour, and the increases across the H100 and three other NVIDIA GPU models, the H200, B200 and B300, ranged from 17% to 21%.

So the public index can see price increases; what the index sees are increases in listed prices. The index is calculated by GPU model, and in the week of October 12, 21 of 26 models rose; getdeploying hasn't broken out which providers changed prices or how much each contributed.

...

The gap is actually less than ten times.

Prices lined up by contract length.

| Contract | Price, autumn 2026 | Term, and whether the customer can leave early | Source of the figure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pay-as-you-go listed | H100 median US$3.51 an hour (40 providers); specialist GPU clouds US$4.50; big clouds such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google US$7.89; Silicon Data's specialist-cloud H100 rental index US$2.82 on October 17, +6.4% over seven days | Stop at any time | Third-party compilation of listed prices |
| One-year contract | H100 US$1.70 → US$2.35 an hour (October 2025 to March 2026) | One year | Silicon Data figures cited by SemiAnalysis |
| Three-to-six-month contract | CoreWeave about US$40 million per MW per year, about US$7.6 to US$8.4 per GPU per hour | Three to six months | Company-reported |
| Cancellable big order | Google pays SpaceX US$920 million a month to rent 110,000 GB200s, about US$11.6 per GPU per hour, about US$55 million to US$60 million per MW per year | Three years on paper, cancellable on 90 days' notice | Four outlets report the same figures; unit price estimated by SecondSource |
| Five-to-six-year contract | IREN–NVIDIA about US$11.3 million; IREN–Microsoft about US$9.7 million; Nebius–Microsoft at least US$11.6 million; OpenAI–Oracle about US$13.3 million; Nscale–Anthropic about US$16 million (six years); all per MW per year | Five to six years, 20% to 30% prepaid | Press releases, filings and reporting; calculated by SecondSource |
| CoreWeave company-wide average | About US$6.9 million to US$8.2 million per MW per year | All contracts | SecondSource's rough calculation |

...

Details of the public index. Each week getdeploying records every provider's pay-as-you-go listed price. getdeploying takes a median for each provider and then a median across providers, one vote per provider, leaving out reserved and spot prices. SecondSource recomputed October 12 against September 14 from getdeploying's public weekly data: the median change across the 26 models is 8.6%, and against October 13, 2025 it is 18.2%. Nebius's new prices from October 1 were reported by the press by September 17 (Investing.com): the H100 from US$3.85 to US$4.50, the H200 from US$4.50 to US$5.40, the B200 from US$7.15 to US$8.50 and the B300 from US$7.85 to US$9.50. Several outlets called it the second increase in three months. All five data-center models in the index rose between September 14 and October 12: the H100 from US$3.34 to US$3.51, the H200 from US$4.44 to US$4.86, the B200 from US$6.52 to US$7.99, the B300 from US$7.87 to US$8.99 and the A100 from US$1.75 to US$1.82. The rise is uneven across generations: the H100 is up 5% over four weeks, the B200 up 23%. Compute Desk, another index provider, builds its index from completed transactions. Compute Desk says the B300 pay-as-you-go price rose 17 days in a row to a record on October 15, at about US$7 to US$10 an hour, about 64% above November 2025. That account comes from a single secondhand source. The September 18 call also said that a near-double-digit quarterly rise in the public index in the fourth quarter would mean the two measures had converged. A 9% rise over four weeks is already close, but what rose is the listed price itself.
